summary:
North Kalimantan stands under the national framework of Indonesia, and no trans-specific safety finding is recorded for the province itself. It is assessed at the national score, meaning the risks a trans visitor faces here are the risks carried by the country as a whole.

Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, the provision reaches consensual same-sex relations as well, and reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Protections are absent on paper. Indonesia provides no anti-discrimination or hate-crime provisions based on sexual orientation or gender identity, same-sex marriage is unrecognised, and legal gender recognition requires sex-reassignment surgery plus judicial approval.

A trans traveller has died in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested on drug charges at an Indonesian airport in 2022 while on honeymoon in Bali. During a WhatsApp call, his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; she alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Official policy frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture among nonmilitary threats alongside terrorism and drug addiction. Reporting published on 14 August 2026 describes mobs attacking trans women in several cities in July 2026 with no prosecutions reported, and civil society sources describe conditions as rapidly worsening. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.
tangentialFactors:
Provincial divergence is documented elsewhere in Indonesia. The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national-level morality provisions. Aceh applies Sharia law; two men were publicly caned there for a same-sex relationship in February 2025, and its punishments reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. North Kalimantan carries no equivalent provision in the sources.

Enforcement at national level also takes the form of venue raids. On 22 June 2025, Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

The wider policy direction is hostile. A proposed obscenity article explicitly naming "same sex" is feared to trigger discriminatory regional bylaws. Indonesia has voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity. A 2025 Pew Research Center figure put 93% of Indonesians calling homosexuality morally unacceptable.

Reporting from August 2026 ties the October 2025 decree directly to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as the government codifies anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law.
localsOnly:
Residents of North Kalimantan have no statutory remedy of the anti-discrimination kind: Indonesia has no law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, and hate-crime sentencing enhancements are unavailable on those grounds. A resident dismissed, evicted, or assaulted for being trans must rely on general criminal provisions that do not recognise the bias element.

Legal gender recognition is gated on surgery and a court order. A resident seeking to align official identity documents must undergo sex-reassignment surgery and obtain judicial approval; no administrative route without surgery appears in the sources.

Conversion therapy is widely practised in Indonesia and openly advertised, a service offered to residents and their families rather than to visitors.

An international human-rights analysis lists North Kalimantan among the eight provinces of Indonesia carrying discriminatory provincial regulations. No incident documentation was found for this province, so the practical reach of any such bylaw within North Kalimantan is unrecorded. The current state of the province's own regulations is not stated in the sources.
outOfScopeNotes:
Sources disagree on the maximum penalty for extra-marital sex under the amended penal code. The national country profile gives two years' imprisonment, while the encyclopedic overview of Indonesian LGBT rights gives one year. The discrepancy is unresolved in the inventory.

No trans-specific safety finding, incident record, or law-enforcement data specific to North Kalimantan was located. The province is treated at the national level because nothing unit-specific was documented, not because unit-level data was confirmed to match the national position.

Entry and visa rules, port-of-entry screening, and any treatment of gender markers on foreign passports are not covered by these sources, so no assessment of them for North Kalimantan or Indonesia can be sourced from this inventory.

Whether the July 2026 mob attacks on trans women extended to North Kalimantan is not sourced. The status of the proposed obscenity article naming "same sex", including whether it has been enacted, is likewise unresolved.
